Example 5.4 — hERG liability: which known drugs block the channel?¶

A reproducible record of an AI-assisted BindingDB analysis: each prompt, the BindingDB tool calls that answered it with their recorded results, the answer, and its figures. Run all cells to show the recorded results, or rerun every call on your own copy of the database and check each result against the recorded one.

  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Model: claude-sonnet-5-5
  • Data: BindingDB release 202611 (BDB-mySQL_All_202611_dmp.zip, SHA-256 daea9260d404919a183ce02d91bf4b9c49b410bea7eaaeba105c8e0280510381)
  • Database build: 2026-11-21T01:08:15+00:00, DuckDB 1.5.6
  • Derived data: standard InChIKeys computed from SMILES by RDKit 2026.03.6; compound_property computed from SMILES (largest fragment) by RDKit 2026.03.6
  • Server: mcp-bindingdb v0.1.17, commit 79dae5d22c0f
  • Software: python 3.12.7, duckdb 1.5.6, rdkit 2026.03.6, mcp 2.3.0, gemmi 0.7.5
  • Notebook generated: 2026-11-24T04:55:51Z
  • Contents: 1 exchange · 33 tool calls · 1 figure

How to run¶

Keep the notebook in its folder, which holds everything it needs: requirements.txt (mcp-bindingdb at its commit and the versions of the packages it needs), the recorded results in data/ and the figures in figures/. With uv, from that folder (replace the path with yours):

cd /path/to/5.4-herg-liability-notebook
uv run --no-project --with-requirements requirements.txt --with jupyterlab jupyter lab 5.4-herg-liability-notebook.ipynb

then choose Run → Run All Cells. The first start installs the packages, which takes a minute or two; the cells show the recorded results, so no database is needed. Without uv: pip install -r requirements.txt jupyterlab, then jupyter lab 5.4-herg-liability-notebook.ipynb in the folder.

How to rerun the calls¶

To rerun every BindingDB call on your own copy of release 202611 and check each result against the recorded one, set RERUN = True in the setup cell and run all cells, or rerun the notebook without opening Jupyter, writing a copy with the new results:

cd /path/to/5.4-herg-liability-notebook
BINDINGDB_RERUN=1 uv run --no-project --with-requirements requirements.txt --with nbconvert jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute --output 5.4-herg-liability-notebook-rerun.ipynb 5.4-herg-liability-notebook.ipynb

A rerun needs the database: the one BINDINGDB_DUCKDB=/path/to/bindingdb_202611.duckdb names (put it before uv run), else the newest one mcp-bindingdb built on this computer, for example for Claude Desktop. With neither, the first rerun builds one, which takes about half an hour and 2.4 GB. To build exactly release 202611, with a clone of mcp-bindingdb:

git clone https://github.com/sbl-sdsc/mcp-bindingdb.git
cd mcp-bindingdb
git checkout 79dae5d22c0f15b8ded9b49adc8b105f0463703a
scripts/build_duckdb.sh --release 202611

The setup cell checks the database's release and source checksum against the recorded ones.

Run as it is, each call cell shows its recorded result, read from data/ and checked against the SHA-256 digest recorded in the cell. Rerun, it shows the new result with ✅ when it matches the recorded one (floats to 10 significant digits, ids of viewers and files left out). Calls to PubChem, RCSB or PDBe depend on those services and may differ. The prose answers are the model's and are not recomputed.

In [ ]:
# Shows the results recorded during the session (data/), so the notebook runs without a database. Set
# RERUN = True (or start Jupyter with BINDINGDB_RERUN=1) to rerun every BindingDB call on a local copy of
# the database instead and check it against its recorded result: see 'How to rerun the calls' above.
from mcp_bindingdb.notebook import Replay

RERUN = False
replay = Replay(release='202611', source_zip_sha256='daea9260d404919a183ce02d91bf4b9c49b410bea7eaaeba105c8e0280510381', rerun=RERUN)

Recorded with BindingDB release 202611, mcp-bindingdb v0.1.17 (commit 79dae5d22c0f)
python 3.12.7, duckdb 1.5.6, rdkit 2026.03.6, mcp 2.3.0, gemmi 0.7.5

sql = """
    WITH m(drug, monomerid) AS (VALUES ('astemizole',24226),('ibutilide',50131432),('sertindole',50001786),('dofetilide',50031720),('pimozide',50334150),('haloperidol',21398),('droperidol',50017705),('cisapride',50005836),('thioridazine',50002338),('ziprasidone',50048803),('terfenadine',50017376),('terfenadine',22879),('domperidone',50241107),('risperidone',50001885),('loratadine',22876),('loratadine',50637414),('verapamil',81939),('verapamil',50338982),('verapamil',50005628),('verapamil',50279753),('mesoridazine',50131440),('mesoridazine',50370414),('nilotinib',50237710),('bepridil',78577),('bepridil',50664461),('bepridil',50017667),('ondansetron',85330),('ondansetron',50241365),('ondansetron',50000493),('quinidine',50121975),('quinidine',50017681),('quinidine',50198085),('chlorpromazine',50001888),('fluoxetine',30130),('fluoxetine',50136166),('fluoxetine',50667278),('clozapine',50001884),('clozapine',22869),('citalopram',25870),('citalopram',50302225),('methadone',82507),('methadone',50027393),('amiodarone',18957),('amiodarone',50318906),('fexofenadine',22874),('erythromycin',50344942),('erythromycin',50127141),('moxifloxacin',50366824),('moxifloxacin',50131428),('sotalol',25762)),
    h AS (SELECT m.drug, a.affinity_type, a.value, a.p_affinity FROM m JOIN activity a USING (monomerid)
          WHERE a.uniprot = 'Q12809' AND a.uniprot_raw = a.uniprot AND a.organism = 'Homo sapiens' AND a.relation = '=' AND a.affinity_type IN ('Ki','Kd','IC50'))
    SELECT drug, count(*) n_all, median(value) med_all, min(value) best_all,
     count(*) FILTER (WHERE affinity_type='IC50') n_ic50, median(value) FILTER (WHERE affinity_type='IC50') med_ic50, min(value) FILTER (WHERE affinity_type='IC50') best_ic50,
     count(*) FILTER (WHERE affinity_type='Ki') n_ki, median(value) FILTER (WHERE affinity_type='Ki') med_ki,
     count(*) FILTER (WHERE affinity_type='Kd') n_kd, median(value) FILTER (WHERE affinity_type='Kd') med_kd
    FROM h GROUP BY drug ORDER BY med_ic50 NULLS LAST
    
"""

Figure 1: Known drugs that block hERG (KCNH2) below 1 µM. (as recorded)

🧠 Assistant

First, a limitation to state up front: BindingDB has no "approved drug" flag. It records measurements, not regulatory status. So there is no query that returns "approved drugs". What I did instead was check a list of 30 drugs known for cardiac or QT-interval issues against BindingDB by name. A systematic answer would need an external source of approved drugs (DrugBank, ChEMBL's max_phase) joined on InChIKey.

The scale of the hERG data. Human KCNH2 (UniProt Q12809) has 18,767 measurements on 14,872 compounds from 2,018 sources: one of the most-screened targets in the database, because every drug programme tests for it.

The drugs that bind below 1 uM. 19 of the 30 drugs have a median below 1 uM on human wild-type KCNH2 (exact Ki, Kd and IC50 values pooled). Figure 1 shows the 12 most potent, from astemizole (5 nM) to domperidone (162 nM), with each drug's therapeutic class. The 12 structures share no common core (their largest common substructure has only 6 atoms), so the figure draws them unaligned. Every bar is the median of that drug's exact IC50 values, the one measurement type all of them have; the note gives the number of values and the best one. The remaining drugs, by their median over all exact Ki, Kd and IC50 values:

Median on hERG Drugs
160 nM - 1 uM (not in the figure) risperidone 167 nM, loratadine 172 nM, verapamil 200 nM, mesoridazine 324 nM, nilotinib 371 nM, bepridil 550 nM, ondansetron 813 nM
1 - 10 uM quinidine 1.4 uM, chlorpromazine 1.5 uM, fluoxetine 1.5 uM, clozapine 3.1 uM, citalopram 4.0 uM, methadone 9.8 uM (one value)
10 uM or weaker amiodarone 10 uM, fexofenadine 23 uM, erythromycin 39 uM, moxifloxacin 129 uM
No hERG data sotalol

This list contains two very different things. Astemizole, terfenadine and cisapride were withdrawn or restricted for QT prolongation and torsades de pointes, and their hERG affinity is the reason. But dofetilide and ibutilide are antiarrhythmics whose therapeutic mechanism IS blocking this channel: potent hERG binding is what they are for. The antipsychotics (haloperidol, droperidol, pimozide, sertindole, thioridazine, ziprasidone) carry QT warnings and remain in use with monitoring.

Lesson: affinity alone does not tell you the risk, and the median matters. What determines cardiac risk is the margin between the hERG IC50 and the free drug concentration reached in plasma, not the IC50 by itself. Terfenadine was withdrawn while fexofenadine, its active metabolite and a far weaker blocker (median 23 uM), replaced it. Note also how far the best value sits from the median: terfenadine's best IC50 is 8.9 nM against a median of about 130 nM; amiodarone ranges from 30 nM to 10 uM across five measurements; and erythromycin has a best value of 39 nM against a median of 39 uM, a spread that suggests one of its three entries is out of line with the others. The measurement type moves the numbers too: clozapine's nine IC50s have a median of 324 nM, its four Ki values a median of 10.5 uM. hERG IC50 depends strongly on the assay (patch clamp versus binding displacement, temperature, pulse protocol), so with 2,018 different sources the spread is wide. Quoting a single best value from the literature would move several of these drugs by more than tenfold.

How this was answered

  • search_targets for KCNH2 (Homo sapiens): found human Q12809 (polymerid 2132).
  • run_sql on activity: counted the measurements, compounds and sources for that target.
  • chemical_name_to_smiles for each of the 30 hand-chosen drug names: resolved each name to its structure and BindingDB records (the clozapine and moxifloxacin names each match a second record with a different InChIKey, a tautomer or an unspecified-stereo drawing of the same drug, which I pooled).
  • run_sql over those records: took, per drug, the median and best of the exact values on human wild-type KCNH2 (uniprot_raw = uniprot), over all Ki, Kd and IC50 values and over IC50 alone, with the count of measurements.
  • draw_structure_grid with one card per drug and its IC50 median as the bar, for the 12 most potent.
